title: UK-India Personal Cargo Demand Surges as Diaspora Prepares for Diwali Season
excerpt: Cargo Force reports double-digit growth projections after completing 52,000 shipments in two years, with demand rising in Tier II and III Indian cities.
body:
• Cargo Force, a UK-India cross-border logistics provider, projects double-digit shipment growth over the next 12 to 18 months, fuelled by the UK-India Free Trade Agreement that took effect on July 15, 2026.
  • The company completed more than 52,000 shipments over the past two years with a 95% delivery success rate, averaging 26,000 shipments annually.
  • Demand is rising beyond traditional hubs of Delhi and Mumbai, with cities like Ahmedabad, Chandigarh, Pune, Jaipur, Lucknow and Kochi emerging as key destinations.
  • IAG Cargo is expanding its UK-India network to 70 weekly flights this winter, adding a third daily London-Delhi service from September 2026.

The Diwali Shipping Rush Begins

For the nearly 1.9 million people of Indian origin living in the United Kingdom, the weeks before Diwali are marked not only by festival preparations but by a quieter ritual: packing boxes of gifts, clothes, sweets and household goods to send home to family across India.

Cargo Force, a cross-border logistics provider specializing in the UK-India corridor, says it is seeing a strong uptick in personal cargo demand ahead of the Diwali season. The company projects double-digit growth in shipment volumes over the next 12 to 18 months, according to Stat Times.

"The UK-India corridor remains a key market for us, and we are witnessing growing demand driven by stronger trade ties, increasing cross-border activity, and a large diaspora presence."

— Asad Ali Mirza, Director, Cargo Force

FTA Fuels the Pipeline

The growth projection comes on the heels of the UK-India Free Trade Agreement, which entered into force on July 15, 2026. The deal — the UK's third largest after Australia and Japan — is expected to boost bilateral trade by an additional £25.5 billion annually by 2040, according to the UK government.

For personal cargo and small-business shipments, the FTA lowers trade barriers and simplifies customs processes. Cargo Force says the agreement is expected to boost shipments particularly from emerging cities beyond traditional metro markets.

Over the past two years, the company completed more than 52,000 shipments while maintaining a 95% delivery success rate, despite undergoing a major technology migration. Shipment categories span personal effects, household goods, gifts, e-commerce parcels, SME exports and business consignments.

Beyond Delhi and Mumbai

A notable shift is where the packages are going. Cargo Force reports rising demand from Tier II and III Indian cities — Ahmedabad, Chandigarh, Pune, Jaipur, Lucknow, Coimbatore, Kochi, Indore and Surat — reflecting broader economic development and increasing international trade activity beyond the major metros.

The trend mirrors wider changes in the UK-India logistics corridor. IAG Cargo is expanding its network to 70 weekly UK-India flights this winter, up from 56 in 2025. A third daily London Heathrow-Delhi service launches September 19, operated by British Airways on a Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner. Between January and May 2026, IAG Cargo recorded a 12.6% increase in outbound cargo from Delhi and a 14.4% rise in inbound shipments, according to Container News.

What It Costs

Personal cargo services like Cargo Force offer flat rates that undercut traditional courier services. The company advertises rates starting at £4 per kilogram for door-to-door service from the UK to India, covering customs duties. For British Indian families sending Diwali gifts, the economics are straightforward: a 10-kilogram box of clothes and sweets costs roughly £40 to ship, arriving within a week or two.

Looking Ahead

The personal cargo corridor is expected to strengthen as the FTA takes full effect. With annual remittance flows between the UK and India estimated at $12-13 billion, the physical movement of goods is a parallel expression of diaspora connection. As Diwali approaches — falling on October 20 this year — British Indians are already booking shipments early to beat the seasonal rush.
nri_angle: Nearly 1.9 million British Indians regularly ship gifts, household goods and personal effects to family in India, and the pre-Diwali surge is the busiest period of the year.
